passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against the Desert by the Sea’ (verse 1). Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev, an invader comes from a land of terror.

A dire vision is shown to the prophet. The traitor still betrays, the destroyer still destroys, and Elam and Media are told to go up and lay siege (verse 2). The vision shakes him. ‘Therefore my body is filled with anguish. Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor’ (verse 3). His heart falters, and what he longed for has turned to horror (verse 4).

Meanwhile the princes feast: they set the table, spread the carpet, eat and drink. Then the call comes to rise and oil the shields (verse 5).

The Lord tells him to post a lookout to report what he sees (verse 6), chariots and horsemen, riders on donkeys and camels (verse 7). The lookout keeps watch day after day, night after night (verse 8). Then the riders come, and one answers: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” (verse 9).

‘O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Babylon returns. The oracles against the nations began with Babylon in chapter 13, and chapter 21 announces its fall again, through the eyes of a shaken prophet who feels the vision in his body.

The Desert by the Sea is a riddling title for Babylon, which lay in the flat lands of southern Mesopotamia near the marshes and the head of the Persian Gulf. Elam lay east of Babylonia, and Media to the northeast. Which fall of Babylon is meant is debated. Many link it to Cyrus's capture of Babylon in 539 BC, since the Persians came from the old Elamite region and ruled the Medes, and the feasting princes recall Belshazzar's feast on the night Babylon fell. Others place it in Isaiah's own time, when Babylon under Merodach-baladan rebelled against Assyria with Elamite support and fell to Sargon II around 710 BC and to Sennacherib in 689 BC. On that reading Babylon's fall would have dashed the hopes of those in Judah who saw it as an ally.

The threshing floor was where grain was beaten to separate it from the husk. Judah is pictured as crushed there. The chapter is full of watching and waiting, which suits a people waiting to learn whether any power could rescue it.
passages.later: Revelation takes up the cry of verse 9: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (Revelation 18:2), and ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great’ (Revelation 14:8). Daniel tells of the feast on the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5:30). And Habakkuk stands like this lookout: ‘I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts’ (Habakkuk 2:1).
passages.hard:
Which fall of Babylon does this chapter describe, and why does it matter?

Scholars disagree. One view links the chapter to 539 BC, when Cyrus, ruling the Medes and coming from the Elamite region, took Babylon, and notes the parallel with Belshazzar's feast in Daniel 5. Those who hold this view differ over whether Isaiah foresaw it from the eighth century or whether the oracle comes from a later prophet in Isaiah's tradition. Another view places it in Isaiah's own lifetime, when Babylon fell to Assyria in about 710 or 689 BC, and argues that the prophet's distress in verses 3 and 4 makes more sense if Babylon's fall was bad news for Judah. Each view accounts for some details better than the other.

These notes take no side. The chapter's message is the same on either reading: the gods of Babylon cannot save it, and the people of God, crushed on the threshing floor, must look to the LORD of Hosts.
passages.asks: The lookout stood on the watchtower day after day, night after night, until the news came. Ask what you are waiting for God to show you. And ask whether your hopes are pinned on any power that could fall in a night.

passages.t: Watchman, what is left of the night?
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Dumah’ (verse 11). Someone calls to the prophet from Seir: ‘Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?’ (verse 11).

The watchman replies, ‘Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Dumah was an oasis in northern Arabia, probably modern Dumat al-Jandal, and Seir is the mountain country of Edom, south of the Dead Sea. The name Dumah also sounds like the Hebrew word for silence.

The question is the cry of people in a long night of trouble, under Assyrian pressure: how much longer? The answer is cryptic. Morning is coming, but so is night. Relief will come, and more trouble after it. The invitation is open: ask again, come back again.

The first hearers, and every reader since, have heard in this short exchange the question of anyone in a dark time, and an answer that does not lie.
passages.later: A psalm waits in the same way: ‘My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning’ (Psalm 130:6).
passages.asks: The question from Seir is how much of the night is left. Ask what night you are in, and whether you have asked God how long. And ask whether you can accept an honest answer that promises morning and does not hide the night.

passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Arabia’ (verse 13). The caravans of Dedan must camp in the thickets. ‘Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema; meet the refugees with food’ (verse 14). They are fleeing from the sword, the drawn sword and the bent bow and the stress of battle (verse 15).

The Lord says that within one year, ‘as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone’ (verse 16). The archers of Kedar will be few. ‘For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Dedan and Tema were oasis towns on the caravan routes of northwest Arabia. Kedar was a powerful confederation of Arab tribes in the Syrian and Arabian desert. Assyrian kings campaigned against the Arab tribes repeatedly, including Sargon II and Sennacherib. Later the Babylonian king Nabonidus lived at Tema for about ten years.

The call to bring water and bread to the refugees is striking. In the desert, hospitality to the fugitive was a matter of life and death. Even in an oracle of judgment, the prophet calls for mercy to those fleeing.

The hired worker's year, as in 16:14, is an exact count. Kedar's glory will end on time.
passages.later: The law told Israel, ‘you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 10:19). Jeremiah later speaks of the same tribes in his oracles (Jeremiah 49:28).
passages.asks: Tema is told to bring water to the thirsty and food to the refugees. Ask who is fleeing near you, and what water and bread you could bring. And ask whether you think judgment on a people cancels the duty of mercy to them.
